The interest is not to propose a faithful modeling of the system, but to show in an example how modeling of the material response allows to access relevant microscopic parameters. In the simplified sticky Rouse model [29, 21] the material is represented through a linear chain composed of N monomers. A part of this monomers has a certain relaxation time 𝜏, and another part of the monomers (𝑁') has a slower relaxation time (𝜏'). The slower monomers represent the dynamic links between the different chains that compose the network. The fingerprint of this model is the transition where the moduli G' and G" are parallel with a one-half exponent power law behavior, both near the glass transition and at the beginning of the vitrimeric relaxation.  Considering the response 𝐺O(𝜔) at  180 ºC (Fig 6b), the physical parameters that we can extract are: the ratio between the two plateaus providing N/Nx (in this case ≃ 150), meaning the ratio between free monomers and dynamically crosslinked ones; the extension of the second Rouse regime (before the

13 
beginning of the terminal relaxation with 1 and 2 exponents) giving the number of dynamic crosslinks permanently connected Nx (in this case ≃ 14 ± 6).  The main simplification made in this model is to consider that the network is a dynamic assemble of linear chains, neglecting any branching of the permanently connected structures (see SI for some additional details on the modeling). A detailed topological analysis starting from the basic macromolecules (Fig. 1) which would predict the topological characteristic of the network, goes beyond the scope of this work and will be studied in a following paper [30]. For the moment we only anticipate that the task to predict the network topology, and in particular the number of permanently connected dynamic crosslinks, is not trivial and has a great impact on the mechanical properties of the network, and that an approach that combines solid-state and fluid-state rheology and modeling is promising to access this kind of information and rationalize the response of the system on physical bases.  4. Conclusions In the first part of the paper we investigate the solid state and fluid state viscoelastic properties of a recently developed high Tg vitrimer [20Errore. Il segnalibro non è definito.] using torsional rheology. We obtain the variations of the elastic modulus as function of the temperature and we determine the glass transition temperature. We also demonstrate that the material exhibits terminal relaxation and is indeed a vitrimeric material. The mechanical properties (in particular the capability to relax the stress) are thermally stable at processing temperatures, and we obtain the shift factors as function of the temperature and two activation energies.  In the second part of the paper, we combine this information to discuss the applicability of TTS. We show that we can collapse the data onto a single master curve, at the same time we identify two different relaxation mechanisms (glassy and vitrimeric). The shift factors can be either described by a WLF or by a double Arrhenius. What is the more appropriate approach between the two is actually debated in the literature, and the correct answer is expected to be system dependent. In our case, in terms of temperature the glassy regime is relatively close to the vitrimeric one, so it is not possible to say if the deviations from Arrhenius are only due to an interplay with the glassy dynamics, or to the fact that we only capture the beginning of the vitrimeric regime. It is anyhow evident that two processes are present, and so it seems more meaningful to describe the shift factors with two distinct activation energies.  The presence of different mechanism with different temperature dependence makes the material thermo-rheologically complex, and thus time temperature equivalence fails. We can explain the fact that nonetheless the data collapse in a single master curve as follows. Indeed the two relaxation processes are well enough separated (in frequencies), as compared to our measuring frequency window, and thus in our experiments we never detect the two processes at the same time:  we detect either the glassy modes, or the rubbery plateau (no relaxation), or the terminal vitrimeric relaxation. This observation reconciliates the contradiction found in literature and presented in the introduction.

14 
The shift factors 𝛼(𝑇), give us the temperature dependence of the two processes; the master curve gives us the distribution of relaxation modes Hm(𝜔), from which we separate and characterize the two families of relaxation modes. With these two elements we can recombine the two modes each one with its own temperature dependence to obtain the mechanical response at any temperature.  This methodology, based on standard tools of linear rheology, extends the state-of-the-art rheological practice that in case of thermo-rheological complexity does not provide a modeling of the temperature dependent response over a wide frequency range.  Finally, the viscoelastic moduli (Fig. 6b) are compared with the simplified sticky Rouse model that gives access to some relevant topological parameters of the network.   To summarize, we stress at first the importance of rheological measurement also in the solid regime, to obtain a complete characterization of the relaxation modes originating the mechanical response of the system. These measurements are made possible thanks in torsional rheology. Secondly, we stress the fact that the methodology of measurements and analysis that we presented in this paper opens the path to compare the mechanical response to microscopic models.  6. ABSTRACT: Vitrimers are a class of polymer networks featuring dynamic
covalent cross-links that can undergo associative bond exchange. There has
been recent interest in these materials due to their promise as recyclable
thermosets or self-healing polymers because of the ability of vitrimer
networks to rearrange at the molecular level and undergo macroscopic
flow. However, the practical use of these materials often occurs in the
supercooled regime or glassy state, where the implications of dynamic
bonds are complicated by the interplay between slow activated segmental
dynamics, cross-link (i.e., bond-exchange) kinetics, and ultimately material
properties. In this paper, we combine coarse-grained molecular dynamics
simulation and microscopic statistical mechanical theory to understand
how cross-linking kinetics affect material dynamics and how this couples to segmental relaxation of the polymeric network strands
across a spectrum of length and time scales, especially in the supercooled regime. We characterize the Kuhn segmental alpha
relaxation time and bond exchange time for vitrimer systems across various cross-link densities, temperatures, and bond exchange
rates. Simulation and theory both exhibit a bending-up behavior for bond exchange time upon cooling, suggesting a coupling
between bond exchange dynamics and segmental relaxation that intensifies with faster bond exchange kinetics. We also found bond
exchange dynamics have an impact on Kuhn segment alpha relaxation time, which is most significant at higher cross-link densities.
Both these effects are most prominent when the bond exchange time is similar to the Kuhn segment alpha relaxation time, and the
resulting coupling of these two relaxation processes is tied to both the probability of a free end to find a bonded pair and the time
scale of the constraints imposed by the dynamic cross-links. This relationship is reflected by a cross-link dependence of a theoretical
parameter which represents the quantitative degree of coupling between bond exchange and segmental dynamics. Overall, the
combination of simulation and theory clarifies the intricate interaction between bond kinetics and segmental relaxation and
demonstrates the ability to provide molecular-level insights into vitrimer dynamics over a wide temperature range.

scopic dynamics and the viscoelastic properties of vitrimers.
Despite the ability of hybrid MD/MC simulations to model
vitrimers, these models may require making prescriptive
assumptions of bond dynamics as it requires a user-specified
reaction rate for the MC steps that model bond swapping
events, complicating their application to nonequilibrium
systems.
59
Alternative approaches for modeling dynamic
bonds in glassy polymers were used by Ciarella et al.,
33,60
who used both MD simulations and mode-coupling theory
(MCT) to probe structural relaxation time and found that
fragility can be tuned over an unprecedentedly broad range by
bulk density. This approach notably used a potential that was
originally proposed by Sciortino,
61
with bond swapping
dynamics modeled by incorporating a coordination-dependent
three-body potential that allows the formation of a second
bond and the subsequent bond exchange. This three-body
potential has been successfully implemented to study stress
relaxation and self-healing behaviors, as well as the segmental
relaxation of vitrimers.
33,62−64
Despite this progress, the
fundamental question of how segmental dynamics are affected
by dynamic cross-linking, especially in the supercooled regime,
still needs to be addressed to advance the design and
optimization of vitrimer-based materials.
We have recently used MD simulation and a statistical
mechanical theoretical approach to understand how cross-
linking impacts segmental relaxation and the glass transition
temperature in permanent networks, in collaboration with
experimentalists.
65
Motivated by the poly(n-butyl acrylate)
(PnBA) networks used in experiments, we constructed a
coarse-grained simulation model to reflect the polymer
chemistry.
65
In concert with the elastically collective nonlinear
Langevin equation (ECNLE) theory developed by two of the
current authors and their collaborators, we demonstrated
several findings related to the dynamic consequences of
chemical cross-linking.
65
Most importantly, tight cross-linking
was shown to result in a very large increase in the segmental
relaxation time and glass transition temperature T
g
, with near
quantitative agreement between experiment, simulation, and
theory.
65
This comparison was aided by a remarkable collapse
of Angell plots of the alpha relaxation time for all cross-link
densities, despite the disparity of the alpha time criteria
adopted to define T
g
which spans the weakly (simulation) to
intermediate (experiment) to deeply supercooled (theory)
regimes.
65
Connection to ECNLE theory provided a
mechanistic understanding of the experimental and simulation
observations by showing that structural relaxation involves
coupled local cage scale segment hopping and spatially longer-
range collective elasticity physics, with the latter becoming
more dominant upon cooling.
65
Recently, ECNLE theory has been extended to address the
effect of dynamic cross-linking in vitrimers in a self-consistent
manner, referred to below as SC-ECNLE theory. Based on the
crossover time extracted from the experiments on ethylene
vitrimers
37
at higher temperatures and its Arrhenius extrap-
olation to low temperatures as an input, the theory found good
agreement with experiments regarding several key behaviors:
(i) the vitrimer bond exchange time follows an Arrhenius law
at high enough temperatures, but upward non-Arrhenius
deviations emerge in the deeply supercooled regime, (ii) a
collapsed master curve of Kuhn segmental alpha time for
different temperatures and cross-link densities is predicted if
plotted as a function of T
g
/T, while no such collapse is
observed for vitrimer bond exchange times, (iii) only a small
change in the glass transition temperature (T
g
) is found for
vitrimers with dramatically different bond exchange rates.
66
However, a simulation study is needed to provide further tests
of this theory and to address the effects of material-specific
cross-linker chemistries and, to some extent, dynamic
heterogeneity effects which were ignored in the proposed
theory.
66
In this paper, we employ MD simulation with the potential
proposed by Sciortino
61
to study the glass transition and
structural relaxation in vitrimers over a wide range of
temperatures, cross-link densities, and rates of bond exchange
reactions, with an overarching goal to understand the coupling
between bond exchange and segmental relaxation rates.
Simulation details and theoretical background are given in
Sections 2 and 3, respectively. All results and discussion are
presented in Section 4 including both the simulation results
and theoretical predictions. We first study how the glass
transition temperature T
g
of vitrimers is affected by system
parameters. The effect of bond exchange on the Kuhn segment
alpha relaxation process is then analyzed, followed by a study

5. CONCLUSIONS
In this paper, we used coarse-grained MD simulation to study
the structural relaxation and glass transition in vitrimers, a class
of covalently adaptive networks with dynamic cross-links that
undergo exchange via an associative mechanism. Our model
uses realistic parameters motivated by the chemistries
employed by our experimental collaborators, with a three-
body potential adopted from the literature
56
that allows one to
systematically tune the rate of bond exchange via the
parameter λ and the cross-link density f
cross
. We first quantified
the glass transition temperature
T g , as a function of the cross-
link density f
cross
and bond exchange barrier via the parameter
λ. Then, by quantifying the time scales for both bond exchange
(
bond ) and segmental dynamics (
K, ) as a function of inverse
temperature
T1/ , we investigated the coupling between these
two dynamic processes and how it governs the observed
T g .
Our work demonstrates that slow bond exchange kinetics
behave essentially identically to permanent cross-links, with a
linear increase in

f cross

we considered both the kinetics of bond-exchange events via

The comparison of theory and simulation also indicates that

elementary bond exchange rates appear to largely affect the
alpha time in the intermediate temperature regime at high
cross-link densities, not at low cross-link density regimes or at
very low temperatures. If the bond exchange rate becomes fast
enough, the vitrimer alpha time will be different from that of
the analogous permanent network, and the collapse behavior of
the bond or alpha times in the deeply supercooled regime will
not occur, as recently predicted.
66
The importance of the Kuhn segmental alpha relaxation
process on the bond exchange dynamics, or vice versa, suggests
directions for future study. For example, molecular features
such as the structure and functionality of the cross-linker, or
the spatial correlations between cross-linking groups, will likely
have quantitative effects on vitrimer dynamics. In addition, we
are particularly interested in the effects of glassy dynamics and
bond exchange in vitrimers on the diffusive transport of
molecular penetrants. We have shown in our previous
works
72,83,84,101
that penetrant diffusion in dense permanent
networks is primarily governed by cross-link-dependent
segmental relaxation of the neighboring polymer matrix and
secondarily by network mesh confinement. In vitrimers,
dynamic cross-linking allows the rearrangement of network
topology and can potentially alleviate constraints imposed by
mesh confinement. However, this work suggests that the
segmental relaxation itself would be sensitive to bond exchange
processes on similar time scales and that it may be possible to
engineer vitrimer-based membranes to exhibit selective
transport by controlling these local dynamics. This may be
especially dramatic if the penetrant participates in the exchange
reaction. Indeed, recent experimental findings
24
on the
diffusion of two aromatic dyes with nearly identical sizes�
one dye capable of participating in a reversible reaction with
cross-linkers, while the second remained inert�have revealed
a significant slowdown in diffusion for the reactive dye
depending on bond exchange kinetics.
